paragraphs.paragraph: The psalm opens with a plea for deliverance. David asks God to defend him from enemies, workers of iniquity, and bloody men who seek his life.
paragraphs.title: The Plea for Rescue

easy.explanation: David asks God to deliver him from his enemies and defend him from those who rise against him.
easy.q: What does David ask God to do for him?

answers: Workers of iniquity and bloody men
easy.explanation: He asks to be delivered from workers of iniquity and bloody men.
easy.q: From whom does David ask to be saved?

easy.explanation: David says that they lie in wait for his soul.

medium.explanation: The mighty are gathered against David and seek his life.
medium.q: How are David’s enemies described in these verses?

answers: He has not transgressed or sinned
medium.explanation: David says the enemies gather against him not for his transgression or sin.
medium.q: What does David say about his own conduct?

medium.explanation: David asks God to protect him from those who rise against him.
medium.q: What does the word “defend” mean in this context?

answers: They pursue him, though he claims no transgression
They praise him, though he rejects them
They defend him, though he attacks them
challenge.explanation: David says his enemies gather against him even though he has not sinned or transgressed.
challenge.q: What contrast appears between David and his enemies?

answers: To emphasize the seriousness of his danger
challenge.explanation: The repeated pleas emphasize that David faces a grave threat.
challenge.q: Why does David repeat requests for deliverance and salvation?

challenge.explanation: The expression identifies them as violent men who threaten David’s life.
challenge.q: What does “bloody men” reveal about the enemies?

paragraphs.idea: The psalm opens with a plea for deliverance. David asks God to defend him from enemies, workers of iniquity, and bloody men who seek his life.

paragraphs.paragraph: David’s enemies lie in wait and prepare themselves to harm him, although he has done no wrong. He calls upon the LORD to awaken, behold his situation, and visit the wicked transgressors.
paragraphs.title: The Enemies’ Pursuit and David’s Appeal to God

easy.explanation: David says, “they lie in wait for my soul.”
He says, “They run and prepare themselves without my fault.”
easy.q: What does David say about his fault?

easy.explanation: David calls upon the LORD to awake to help him.
easy.q: Whom does David ask to awaken?

medium.explanation: David emphasizes that the enemies prepare themselves against him without his fault.
medium.q: Why does David consider the attack unjust?

medium.explanation: He asks God to awake to help him and behold what is happening.
medium.q: What does David ask God to do after awakening?

answers: Take notice of and act toward
medium.explanation: God is asked to visit the heathen by taking notice of their wickedness and judging it.
medium.q: What does “visit” mean in this passage?

answers: It shows why he asks God to judge the attackers
It proves he wants to escape judgment
It shows he trusts the enemies
challenge.explanation: Because David says he has no fault, he asks God to see the injustice and respond.
challenge.q: How does David’s claim of innocence support his appeal?

answers: Urgency and a plea for immediate help
challenge.explanation: The word expresses David’s urgent desire for God to act.
David asks God to visit the wicked transgressors.
challenge.q: How are the enemies characterized at the end of the range?

paragraphs.idea: David’s enemies lie in wait and prepare themselves to harm him, although he has done no wrong. He calls upon the LORD to awaken, behold his situation, and visit the wicked transgressors.

paragraphs.paragraph: The enemies return at evening, make a noise like dogs, and go around the city. They speak threateningly as though no one hears them, but the LORD laughs at them and holds the heathen in derision.
paragraphs.title: Enemies Like Dogs Threatening the City

easy.explanation: The verse says, “They return at evening.”
They make a noise like a dog and go around the city.
easy.q: What animal are they compared to?

easy.explanation: The LORD shall laugh at them and hold the heathen in derision.
easy.q: How does the LORD respond to them?

medium.explanation: The verse says they make a noise like a dog and go round about the city.
medium.q: What do the enemies do around the city?

medium.explanation: The verse says, “swords are in their lips,” describing their threatening speech.
medium.q: What do the enemies have in their lips?

medium.explanation: They say, “for who, say they, doth hear?”
medium.q: What question do the enemies ask?

challenge.explanation: The comparison highlights the enemies’ noisy and threatening wandering.
challenge.q: What does the comparison to dogs emphasize?

answers: They threaten, but the LORD laughs at them
They are silent, but the LORD is afraid
They worship, but the LORD hides
challenge.explanation: The enemies speak threateningly, while the LORD treats them with derision.
challenge.q: What is the contrast between the enemies and the LORD?

answers: They arrogantly think no one will answer them
They are asking for David’s help
They confess that God rules them
challenge.explanation: Their question suggests that they act as though no one hears or can respond to them.
challenge.q: What does “who hears?” suggest about the enemies’ attitude?

paragraphs.idea: The enemies return at evening, make a noise like dogs, and go around the city. They speak threateningly as though no one hears them, but the LORD laughs at them and holds the heathen in derision.

paragraphs.paragraph: David waits upon God’s strength and trusts Him as his defence. He asks that his enemies be brought down, not immediately slain, but taken in their pride, cursing, and lies so that all may know that God rules.
paragraphs.title: God as David’s Stronghold and Judge

easy.explanation: David says, “Because of his strength will I wait upon thee.”
He asks that the enemies know that God rules in Jacob unto the ends of the earth.
easy.q: What does David ask people to know?

medium.explanation: David says, “Slay them not, lest my people forget.”
medium.q: Why does David ask, “Slay them not”?

medium.explanation: God is David’s protection and stronghold.
medium.q: What does “defence” mean in this passage?

medium.explanation: They are to be taken in their pride, cursing, and lying.

answers: Their downfall should remain a warning
challenge.explanation: David asks that they be scattered and brought down so that the people will not forget.
challenge.q: What purpose does David give for not killing the enemies immediately?

answers: Their pride, cursing, and lying become the means of their capture
Their prayers save them from judgment
challenge.explanation: The passage says they are taken in the pride and sinful words they speak.
challenge.q: How are the enemies’ words connected to their judgment?

answers: That people may know God rules everywhere
That the enemies may gain power
challenge.explanation: The enemies are consumed so that they may know God rules in Jacob unto the ends of the earth.
challenge.q: What is the ultimate purpose of the judgment?

paragraphs.idea: David waits upon God’s strength and trusts Him as his defence. He asks that his enemies be brought down, not immediately slain, but taken in their pride, cursing, and lies so that all may know that God rules.

paragraphs.paragraph: The enemies return at evening, wander about seeking food, and complain when they are not satisfied. David, however, sings of God’s power and mercy and calls Him his defence and refuge in the day of trouble.
paragraphs.title: The Repeated Picture of the Enemies and the Song of Thanks

easy.explanation: They wander up and down for meat.
David says he will sing of God’s power and mercy.
David says God has been his defence and refuge in the day of trouble.
easy.q: What is God to David in the day of trouble?

medium.explanation: The verse says they grudge if they are not satisfied.
medium.q: What do the enemies do when they are not satisfied?

medium.explanation: David says, “I will sing aloud of thy mercy in the morning.”
medium.q: When will David sing aloud of God’s mercy?

answers: The enemies wander, but David sings
The enemies sing, but David hides
The city rejoices, but God is absent
medium.explanation: The enemies continue wandering while David responds with praise and trust.
medium.q: What contrast appears in the conclusion?

challenge.explanation: Their return and wandering show that the threat continues.
challenge.q: What does the repeated evening scene suggest?

answers: He sings of God’s power, mercy, and protection
challenge.explanation: David chooses worship and confidence in God despite the danger.
challenge.q: How does David respond to danger?

answers: God is David’s strength, defence, mercy, and refuge
The city is David’s only protection
challenge.explanation: David repeatedly identifies God as his strength, defence, refuge, and the God of his mercy.
challenge.q: What idea unites the final verses?

paragraphs.idea: The enemies return at evening, wander about seeking food, and complain when they are not satisfied. David, however, sings of God’s power and mercy and calls Him his defence and refuge in the day of trouble.
